choices.text: A reaction in which two unsaturated molecules add to one another to give a cyclic product
The cyclization of a single conjugated acyclic polyene
choices.why: That is an electrocyclic reaction (Section 30.2).

choices.text: The migration of a σ-bonded group across a π system
choices.why: That is a sigmatropic rearrangement (Section 30.7).

choices.text: The addition of HX across a double bond in a ring
choices.why: A cycloaddition joins two unsaturated molecules into a new ring by a pericyclic process.

explanation: A cycloaddition reaction is one in which two unsaturated molecules add to one another to yield a cyclic product. Like electrocyclic reactions, cycloadditions are governed by the orbital symmetry of the reactants.

prompt: In the [4 + 2] Diels–Alder reaction, how many π electrons does the diene contribute?
explanation: The Diels–Alder reaction takes place between a diene (four π electrons) and a dienophile (two π electrons), which is why it is called a [4 + 2] cycloaddition.

prompt: Two alkenes undergo a [2 + 2] cycloaddition on irradiation. How many carbon atoms are in the ring of the product?
explanation: Each alkene contributes its two double-bond carbons, so the [2 + 2] cycloaddition gives a cyclobutane, a four-membered ring.

prompt: What kind of product does the Diels–Alder reaction of a diene with a dienophile give?

choices.text: A cyclohexene
A cyclobutane
choices.why: Cyclobutanes come from photochemical [2 + 2] cycloadditions of two alkenes.

choices.text: A 1,3-cyclohexadiene
choices.why: A cyclohexadiene comes from the electrocyclic ring-closure of a triene. The Diels–Alder product keeps only one C=C bond.

choices.text: A cyclobutene
choices.why: A cyclobutene comes from the electrocyclic ring-closure of a conjugated diene.

explanation: The Diels–Alder cycloaddition is a pericyclic process between a diene (four π electrons) and a dienophile (two π electrons) that yields a cyclohexene product.

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with diethyl maleate (a cis-disubstituted alkene) at room temperature. What is formed?

choices.text: Only the cis-disubstituted cyclohexene
Only the trans-disubstituted cyclohexene
choices.why: The trans product comes from diethyl fumarate, the trans isomer of the dienophile.

choices.text: A mixture of cis and trans cyclohexenes
choices.why: Diels–Alder reactions are stereospecific with respect to substituents; the cis dienophile gives only the cis product.

choices.text: A disubstituted cyclobutane
choices.why: A diene and a dienophile give a six-membered ring, a cyclohexene.

explanation: Diels–Alder reactions are stereospecific. Room-temperature reaction of 1,3-butadiene with diethyl maleate (cis) gives exclusively the cis-disubstituted cyclohexene; diethyl fumarate (trans) gives exclusively the trans product.

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with diethyl fumarate (a trans-disubstituted alkene). What is formed?

choices.text: Only the trans-disubstituted cyclohexene
Only the cis-disubstituted cyclohexene
choices.why: The cis product comes from diethyl maleate, the cis isomer.

choices.text: A mixture of cis and trans cyclohexenes
choices.why: The reaction is stereospecific: the trans relationship of the dienophile's substituents is kept.

choices.text: No reaction, because the substituents are trans
choices.why: Diethyl fumarate does react with 1,3-butadiene; it gives the trans-disubstituted product.

explanation: The Diels–Alder reaction keeps the dienophile's substituent geometry: diethyl fumarate (trans) exclusively yields the trans-disubstituted cyclohexene.

prompt: What happens when two simple alkenes are heated together, and when they are irradiated?

choices.text: Heating gives no [2 + 2] reaction; irradiation gives a cyclobutane
Heating gives a cyclobutane; irradiation gives no reaction
choices.why: This is reversed. The [2 + 2] cycloaddition takes place only on irradiation.

choices.text: Both heating and irradiation give a cyclobutane
choices.why: The [2 + 2] cycloaddition between two alkenes does not occur thermally.

choices.text: Heating gives a cyclohexene by a Diels–Alder reaction
choices.why: A Diels–Alder reaction needs a diene with four π electrons; two alkenes have only two each.

explanation: In contrast to the [4 + 2] Diels–Alder reaction, the [2 + 2] cycloaddition between two alkenes does not occur thermally. It takes place only on irradiation, yielding cyclobutane products.

choices.text: Bonding between lobes on the same face of one reactant and lobes on the same face of the other
Bonding between lobes on the same face of one reactant and lobes on opposite faces of the other
choices.why: That describes an antarafacial cycloaddition, which needs a twist in one π system.

choices.text: A cycloaddition that can only take place on irradiation
choices.why: Suprafacial describes the geometry of bonding, not the conditions; the thermal Diels–Alder reaction is suprafacial.

choices.text: A cycloaddition that is symmetry-disallowed
choices.why: Both suprafacial and antarafacial cycloadditions are symmetry-allowed.

explanation: Suprafacial cycloadditions take place when lobes on the same face of one reactant bond with lobes on the same face of the other. Antarafacial cycloadditions bond lobes on the same face of one reactant with lobes on opposite faces of the other (Figure 30.5.1).

prompt: Antarafacial cycloadditions are symmetry-allowed. Why, then, are suprafacial cycloadditions much more common for small π systems?

choices.text: An antarafacial reaction needs a twist of the π orbital system in one reactant, which geometric constraints make difficult
Antarafacial cycloadditions are actually symmetry-disallowed
choices.why: Both suprafacial and antarafacial cycloadditions are symmetry-allowed.

choices.text: Antarafacial cycloadditions occur only with alkynes
choices.why: The problem is geometric: one π system must twist.

choices.text: Antarafacial cycloadditions pass through carbocation intermediates
choices.why: Cycloadditions are pericyclic; the difficulty is the twisted geometry, not an intermediate.

explanation: Both suprafacial and antarafacial cycloadditions are symmetry-allowed. Geometric constraints often make antarafacial reactions difficult because the π orbital system of one reactant must twist, so suprafacial cycloadditions are much more common for small π systems.

prompt: Under what conditions do Diels–Alder reactions often take place?

choices.text: Easily, at room temperature or slightly above
Only on irradiation with ultraviolet light
choices.why: The [2 + 2] cycloaddition needs light; the [4 + 2] Diels–Alder reaction occurs thermally.

choices.text: Only when heated far above room temperature for long periods
choices.why: Many Diels–Alder reactions take place easily at room temperature or only slightly above.

choices.text: Only by nonconcerted, high-energy pathways
choices.why: Nonconcerted pathways are for symmetry-disallowed processes. The Diels–Alder reaction is symmetry-allowed.

explanation: Many thousands of Diels–Alder reactions are known. They often take place easily at room temperature or slightly above, and they are stereospecific with respect to substituents.
